messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Mai was forty-two, a project manager for a regional healthcare logistics firm, and married for fifteen years. Two years ago, she was hospitalized for a sudden, severe septic infection following a routine surgery. The illness nearly killed her; she spent ten days in the ICU, drifting in and out of consciousness, tethered to monitors, lines, and a breathing tube. What she remembered most vividly was not the pain but the cold—the relentless, sterile cold of the IV fluids entering her arm, and the sharp, disinfectant smell of the room that seemed to cling to her skin even after she was discharged.

Now, those sensory fragments had become landmines. A whiff of rubbing alcohol in a hallway could stop her mid-sentence, flooding her with a wave of panic that felt like drowning. The cold air from an air-conditioning vent in her office made her flinch, her mind instantly pulling her back to that ICU bed. When she saw a colleague’s insulin pen on a desk, her stomach dropped, and she had to excuse herself to the restroom. Each time a trigger hit, Mai felt the memory surge back—not as a coherent story, but as a fractured, terrifying jolt. Some moments, like the doctor’s face when he told her she might not survive, were excruciatingly clear; others, like the first three days, were a complete, black void. The worst part was that sometimes she would feel the full, crushing emotional intensity of that terror without any image at all—just a raw, disembodied dread that left her shaking.

In response, Mai had developed a rigid set of habits. She avoided hospitals entirely, rescheduling annual physicals and driving an extra twenty minutes to avoid passing the medical center where she had been treated. At work, she monitored her own thoughts constantly, scanning for any hint of the memory or the fear, trying to catch it before it could take hold. She also tried, almost ritually, to erase the memory itself—telling herself it was over, it didn’t matter, it wasn’t real. But these efforts backfired. The more she tried to push the memory away, the more the fragmented, unreal quality of it bothered her. It felt so extreme, so unbelievable, that she sometimes wondered if it had actually happened to her. This sense of unreality, in turn, made her feel like she was losing her grip on reality, which only intensified her thought monitoring and her determination to suppress it.

These strategies also fed a deeper, more corrosive set of beliefs. Mai had come to believe that her life was destroyed by what happened—that she was no longer the capable, reliable person she had once been. She was certain she had failed in her most important role: as a mother to her two teenage children, who had been terrified while she was sick and whom she now felt unable to protect or even fully engage with. Every cold draft or medical smell reminded her that her body was permanently damaged, that she was fundamentally vulnerable. The triggers did not just provoke fear; they confirmed her negative appraisals, reinforcing the idea that she was broken and that her life was over.

The memories themselves strengthened these beliefs. When the story felt unreal, Mai would tell herself that she must be exaggerating, that she was weak for not moving on—which deepened her sense of failure. And when the emotional flashbacks hit without a clear image, she interpreted them as proof that her mind was fundamentally broken. The cycle tightened: a cold gust in the parking lot triggered a memory fragment; that fragment confirmed her belief that her body was ruined; that belief made her scan her thoughts for danger; the scanning triggered a new memory; and the loop began again. Her husband had started to notice her pulling away, and her children had stopped asking her to drive them to activities because she always made excuses. At work, she had begun missing deadlines, her mind constantly occupied with the effort of avoidance.

What finally brought Mai to a therapist’s office was a panic attack in the grocery store, triggered by a shopper wearing a strong floral perfume that reminded her of the hospital’s hand soap. She had fled the aisle, leaving her cart behind, and sat in her car for twenty minutes, unable to stop trembling. She was terrified that she was going crazy, that the memory would eventually swallow her whole. But she was also, quietly, hoping that someone might finally help her believe that it was real—and that she could survive it.
